materials.title: Listen to a talk in a biology class.
materials.transcript: Modern fish farming relies on massive inputs shall feed to boost fish production. This can cause nutrient overload where excessive amounts of uneaten food plus waste products trigger algal blooms. Algal blooms are rapid increases in algae, tiny aquatic plants that can cloud the water. When those algal blooms die off, they decompose and deplete oxygen from the water, which can suffocate fish and other aquatic life. Of course, the main cause of algal blooms is chemical fertilizers in agricultural runoff, like when water from rain or irrigation flows over fields and carries the fertilizers into rivers and coastal waters. But fish farming causes algal blooms too. An intriguing alternative is, or was, the coastal fish ponds of ancient Hawaii, called Loko'ia. People in Hawaii are reviving them today. These ponds, built along the shore using mainly lava, captured nutrient-rich runoff from nearby fields, naturally fertilizing the ponds. This was before the days of concentrated artificial fertilizers. Instead of causing algal blooms, the nutrients supported modest growth of algae, which fed local plant-eating fish. Ponds used natural tidal flushing to bring in fresh seawater and remove waste, which kept oxygen levels stable. And here's the clever part. The special sluice gates connecting the ponds to the ocean had small holes. These holes allowed juvenile fish to swim in from the ocean and fatten up on the food in the pond, but then prevented them from escaping once they matured. So they could be easily harmed.

materials.title: Listen to an art history class.
materials.transcript: When I show students a small bowl by the Native American potter Lucy Lewis, they often say it feels modern, like minimalist almost. Lucy Lewis was a 20th-century Native American artist, and her pottery looks contemporary, but it's anchored in traditional Native American techniques. How so? Well, Lewis learned to build clay pots from women in her community. As a kid, Lewis made pottery for tourists, sold to travelers passing through. She found ideas in publications, books, especially a local painting style that dated back to the 11th century, of traditional black-on-white geometric designs she saw in book illustrations, and she revived that style. Lewis painted black-and-white designs on her plates, bowls, etc. She used fine linework and balanced symmetry to interpret the old designs in a personalized way. As an adult, she became an award-winning artist, but she lived in a remote area in the southwestern United States. Due to her location she didn't have any contact with museums or art collectors, which I mean honestly sounds berating to me. She could create designs she wanted and follow her own inspiration without interference, and these days her pieces are sought after and valuable. Now people sometimes assume that authenticity means keeping exactly to an old way of doing things, which can be true, but Lewis's work suggests authenticity can be procedural. You honor lineage through method, firing, meticulous brush control, while still negotiating new markets and new audiences, honoring your own creativity in the process.

materials.title: Listen to a talk in an ecology class.
materials.transcript: Soil fertility doesn't just depend on minerals or fertilizers. It also depends on microbes, especially bacteria that live around plant roots. These microbes break down organic matter and release nutrients that plants can absorb. But for these processes to work well, bacteria often need to act together, not just individually. One way they coordinate their behavior is through quorum sensing, figuring out if there's enough of them around. Bacteria release and detect chemical signals. Think of it like leaving notes on a shared bulletin board. One note doesn't make much difference. But when enough notes accumulate, everyone in the community notices. That's when the group, the bacteria, shift from working alone to coordinated action. An example of this kind of coordination is the formation of biofilms, sticky communities that cling to soil or root surfaces. Building biofilms benefits both the microbes and plants because it improves the microbes' ability to capture and retain nutrients. But building a biofilm is expensive for the bacteria in energy terms, so it's beneficial for them to wait until there's a large enough group before committing. If they start too early, there may not be enough cells to sustain the structure, which would make it a waste of energy. Quorum sensing helps them decide when it's worth pooling effort. And plants can actually influence this system. Roots release chemical compounds that magnify microbial signals. This helps recruit the helpful microbes that the plants need.

materials.title: Listen to a talk in an art history class.
materials.transcript: Paintings can deteriorate over time. Color can gradually be lost and so on. So let's talk about painting restoration, the ways in which professional conservators bring a painting back to its original glory. The first time I watched a conservator clean a painting, it was really eye-opening. She leaned in with a cotton swab and started moving it across a dark corner, like she was erasing pencil marks. At one point, she lifted off a thin layer of old varnish. Varnish is the originally transparent coating the artist had applied over the finished painting to protect it. But varnish can brown from collecting dirt over time and so can become less transparent. After the varnish was removed, the color under it popped back like someone had turned the lights on. Another part that was super interesting: they sometimes use gels, liquids to clean. A gel holds the cleaning agent in place so it stays put, doesn't soak into cracks or drift into areas you never meant to touch. Think of it as putting the chemistry on a short leash. Now, if this sounds slow, it is. But that slowness is the point. Museums used to prize dramatic before-and-after reveals. But nowadays the goal is more like good editing: remove what doesn't belong, keep what does, and leave a clear record so the next team can undo or improve what you did.
